title: SUSTAINABLE AGRICULTURAL PRACTICES
body_text:
Agriculture is a State subject. The Government is supplementing the efforts of State/UT Government for promoting sustainable agriculture through various schemes and programs. Under these schemes emphasis is being placed on balanced nutrient management, efficient water use, conservation agriculture, integrated farming systems, agroforestry, natural and organic farming, and promotion of climate-resilient agricultural technologies.
Under the Soil Health & Fertility Scheme, assistance is provided to States for promoting Integrated Nutrient Management through the judicious use of fertilizers. This improves fertilizer use efficiency and promotes balanced nutrient application. 26.18 crore Soil Health Cards have been generated so far. To increase water use efficiency at farm level through micro irrigation, Government is implementing Per Drop More Crop Scheme.  Under the scheme, fertigation is also promoted. This enables application of water-soluble fertilizers directly to root zone ensuring precise nutrient delivery. 114.60 lakh hectares has been brought under micro-irrigation, benefitting about 100 lakh farmers.  Organic farming is being promoted through Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (PKVY) and Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North Eastern Region (MOVCDNER) for the North Eastern States. Assistance of Rs. 15,000 per ha is provided to farmers through Direct Benefit Transfer under PKVY and MOVCDNER. PKVY has covered 18.93 lakh hectares, benefiting 33.63 lakh farmers. MOVCDNER has brought 2.36 lakh hectares under organic farming, benefiting 2.74 lakh farmers. Agroforestry Scheme is being implemented to encourage integration of trees with agricultural crops. To ensure availability of quality planting material, financial assistance is provided for setting up of new nurseries and raising of saplings in existing nurseries under Agroforestry Scheme. Financial assistance includes ₹16 lakh for setting up big nurseries (1 ha), ₹10 lakh for small nurseries (0.5 ha), and up to ₹5 lakh per existing nursery for raising saplings is provided under the programme. 826 nurseries have been established and about 1062.18 lakh saplings raised in last 3 years. The National Mission on Natural Farming (NMNF) was approved by the Union Cabinet on 25.11.24 to promote Natural Farming. The Mission strengthens agriculture practices with scientific agro ecological approaches for sustainability, climate resilience and safe food. Under NMNF, 11.81 lakh hectares have been covered in 24,031 clusters, benefiting 24.69 lakh farmers. Incentive support on Rs. 4000/ acre for 2 years is given for farmers to practice Natural Farming, preparation of natural farming inputs or purchase of inputs from Bio-input Resource Centers (BRCs) etc. Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses, National Mission on Edible Oils–Oilseeds (NMEO-OS) and National Food Security Nutrition Mission (NFSNM) & Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture (MIDH) promote crop diversification. Financial assistance/incentives under the Schemes are provided in accordance with the respective operational guidelines of the Schemes.
The Government is implementing the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY) to enhance physical access to water on farms, expand cultivable area under assured irrigation, improve on-farm water-use efficiency and promote sustainable water conservation practices. Under the Har Khet Ko Pani (HKKP) component, the schemes of Surface Minor Irrigation (SMI) and Repair, Renovation and Restoration (RRR) of Water Bodies are being implemented by the Department of Water Resources, River Development and Ganga Rejuvenation, Ministry of Jal Shakti. As reported by the Ministry of Jal Shakti, Central Assistance is provided to States/UTs for creation and restoration of irrigation potential under these schemes. Besides, under Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission – Gramin (VB-G RAM-G), being implemented by the Ministry of Rural Development, water conservation activities are prioritised through Natural Resource Management (NRM) works. These constitute 110 works out of 318 permissible works under the programme, improving water security and conservation.
NITI Aayog has undertaken the evaluation of various schemes being implemented. As per the evaluation reports, under Per Drop More Crop Scheme, 62.46% of farmers reported a substantial increase in water use efficiency or crop yield. Under the Rainfed Area Development Scheme, 70.28% of farmers reported a substantial improvement in farm productivity. The study also reported that 63.78% of farmers adopting soil Health Card recommendations experienced improved fertilizer use efficiency or crop yield, while 68.5% reported improvement in soil health through the use of natural inputs. Under the Organic Farming, 75.85% of farmers reported significant improvements in soil fertility, reduced chemical input costs, or enhanced produce quality. Under the National Mission on Natural Farming, 90.1% of farmers reported reduced input costs compared to the use of chemical fertilizers. The report also highlights the positive contribution of MIDH to farm profitability, livelihood diversification, and long-term capacity building in the horticulture sector. As per the evaluation report, strategic interventions could increase domestic edible oil availability to 16 MT by 2030 and 26.7 MT by 2047, strengthening self-sufficiency in oilseeds.
As reported by Central Ground Water Board, as per the pre-monsoon 2026 assessment, the groundwater situation remains largely stable across the country. Out of 9,085 monitoring wells, 87.8% (7,977 wells) fall under the normal category. These findings indicate that the interventions are contributing to efficient water management, strengthening resource conservation, improving climate resilience and supporting the long-term sustainability of agricultural production systems.
The adoption of sustainable agricultural practices varies across regions depending on agro-climatic conditions, availability of irrigation infrastructure, and local resource endowments. The Government continues to strengthen sustainable agricultural practices through improved irrigation, water conservation, efficient resource management and climate-resilient interventions to integrate sustainability with economic viability and enhance the resilience, competitiveness and long-term growth of the agricultural sector. Despite the challenges posed by biotic and abiotic stresses, the agriculture sector has recorded sustained growth in crop productivity and overall agricultural production over the last decade. Food grain production has increased from 252.03 million tonnes in 2014–15 to a record 357.73 million tonnes in 2024–25, while horticulture production has increased from 280.98 million tonnes in 2014–15 to 370.73 million tonnes in 2024–25, reflecting the resilience and steady growth of agricultural production across the country.
This information was given by the Minister of State for Agriculture and Farmers Welfare SHRI RAMNATH THAKUR in a written reply in Lok Sabha today.
*****
RC/MS

enrichment.summary: In a written Lok Sabha reply on 11 August 2026, the Minister of State for Agriculture and Farmers Welfare detailed Central schemes promoting sustainable agriculture, including Soil Health Cards, Per Drop More Crop, PKVY/MOVCDNER for organic farming, Agroforestry Scheme, and the National Mission on Natural Farming (NMNF). It cited NITI Aayog evaluation data showing high farmer satisfaction across schemes and noted foodgrain production rose from 252.03 million tonnes (2014-15) to 357.73 million tonnes (2024-25), while horticulture output rose from 280.98 to 370.73 million tonnes over the same period.
enrichment.context:
Sustainable agriculture has become a policy priority in India due to concerns over soil degradation, groundwater depletion, and climate change impacts on farm productivity. Since agriculture is a State subject under the Constitution's Seventh Schedule, the Union government uses centrally sponsored schemes to incentivize states toward practices like balanced fertilizer use, micro-irrigation, and organic/natural farming rather than mandating them directly. Key programs mentioned—Soil Health Card scheme, Per Drop More Crop (a PMKSY component), PKVY, and the newer National Mission on Natural Farming (approved by Cabinet in November 2024)—reflect a shift from the Green Revolution's chemical-intensive model toward resource-efficient and ecologically sustainable farming, partly driven by concerns over fertilizer subsidy burden and soil health decline.

This reply also intersects with India's water security and self-reliance goals: PMKSY's Har Khet Ko Pani component and the Rural Development Ministry's VB-GRAM-G scheme link irrigation and water conservation to employment guarantee frameworks (successor to MGNREGA-linked works). The mention of edible oil self-sufficiency targets (16 MT by 2030, 26.7 MT by 2047) ties into India's import dependency on edible oils, a recurring economic and trade policy concern given India imports a majority of its edible oil needs. NITI Aayog's evaluation-based governance approach reflects the broader push for outcome-based scheme monitoring across ministries.

prelims_questions.question: The National Mission on Natural Farming (NMNF), mentioned in a recent Lok Sabha reply, was approved by the Union Cabinet in which year?
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states the National Mission on Natural Farming was approved by the Union Cabinet on 25.11.2024.

prelims_questions.question: Which of the following scheme components promotes 'fertigation', enabling precise nutrient delivery to the root zone through water-soluble fertilizers?
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states that under the Per Drop More Crop Scheme, fertigation is promoted, enabling application of water-soluble fertilizers directly to the root zone.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the key Central government schemes aimed at promoting sustainable agricultural practices in India. Evaluate their effectiveness in improving water use efficiency, soil health, and farm incomes.

Agriculture being a State subject poses challenges for uniform implementation of Centrally Sponsored Schemes. Discuss with reference to sustainable agriculture initiatives like PKVY and National Mission on Natural Farming.
